Women's Rights. The historical struggle to secure legal, political, social, and economic equality for women. Beginning in earnest with the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848 and accelerating through the twentieth century, the movement sought voting rights, educational access, property rights, workplace equality, and reproductive autonomy. The movement achieved major victories—the Nineteenth Amendment granting women's suffrage in 1920, Title Nine mandating educational equality in 1972, and reproductive rights—while continuing to confront persistent inequalities in pay, representation, and social authority.

The Seneca Falls Convention in 1848 in upstate New York was organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. It published the Declaration of Sentiments, a document modeled on the Declaration of Independence asserting women's natural rights and demanding suffrage and legal equality.

The nineteenth-century women's rights movement was led by Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and others. They demanded voting rights, property rights, divorce rights, and educational access, facing ridicule, arrest, and imprisonment for asserting women's equality. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, granted women the right to vote in federal elections, a victory won after decades of agitation, civil disobedience, and political organizing by suffragists.

The Second Wave of feminism from the 1960s to 1980s advanced women's rights through consciousness-raising groups, direct action, and political organizing, demanding equal pay, reproductive rights, and freedom from sexual harassment and domestic violence. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited employment discrimination based on sex, though this protection was initially downplayed. Title Seven became the foundation for workplace equality litigation. Title Nine in 1972 mandated sex equality in education, requiring equal funding and opportunities in school athletics, academics, and extracurricular activities, transforming women's access to sports and higher education.

The Equal Rights Amendment, first proposed in 1923 and passed by Congress in 1972, would have constitutionally prohibited sex discrimination. Though it fell short of the required states' ratification, it galvanized feminist organizing and became a symbol of women's equality.

The legalization of contraception and abortion rights—secured through Griswold v. Connecticut in 1965 and Roe v. Wade in 1973—gave women control over reproduction and enabled greater economic and social autonomy. The Women's Liberation Movement challenged patriarchal assumptions about women's roles, questioning marriage, motherhood, and heterosexuality as compulsory, asserting women's right to self-determination.

Persistent inequalities remain. The gender wage gap, underrepresentation in political office and corporate leadership, disproportionate burden of unpaid domestic and caregiving labor, and violence against women continue to motivate feminist activism.
